land.text: the Fergana Valley, whose Bukharan authority 'was weakening' in the early 18th century

keyframe_review.note: 85,974 km2 for 1709-1787 (68.7-73.8 E, 39.4-42.2 N): the Fergana Valley with Kokand, 'Marghilan, Andijan, Namangan'. Shahrukh Biy 'established the Koktonliq Ata fortress near Kokand' in 1709. Abd al-Rahim Biy 'briefly seized Khujand, Urateppe, and the remains of Samarkand' in the 1720s-30s and was murdered in Khojand in 1734: temporary, not in the shape. Irdana Biy 'temporarily took control of Tashkent in 1765 before Ablay Khan retook it'.
85,753 km2 for 1788-1802: the same Fergana outline within 0.3 percent; no page opened dates a change of 1788 (the Emirate of Bukhara begins in Cliopatria in 1788).
86,046 km2 for 1803-1804, 293 km2 larger than the previous shape: unverified: page budget. The pages give no territorial event for 1803.

85,753 km2 for 1805-1808, the 1788 outline again. Narbuta Biy's and Alim Khan's reigns (1770-1799, 1799-1811) bring 'the western half of the Fergana Valley, taking in Khujand and Tashkent' under Alim, Tashkent in 1809.

174,694 km2 for 1809-1821 (66.8-73.8 E, 39.4-43.8 N): the Fergana Valley plus Tashkent and the Syr Darya lands to Turkestan. The Tashkent page: 'In 1809, Tashkent was annexed to the Khanate of Kokand' (after the independent Tashkent state of Yunus Khoja, 1784-1807). The pages open do not date Sayram, Turkestan and the Syr Darya part of the shape, which the Kazakh dossier also has from 1809.

475,816 km2 for 1822-1847 (65.4-80.8 E, 39.4-45.1 N): Fergana, Tashkent, the Syr Darya to Ak-Mechet, the Talas, Chu and Issyk-Kul country and the south-eastern Kazakh steppe. Infobox '647,497 km2' for the late 1830s: ratio 0.73, within the factor of two; the shape is the smaller. The date 1822 is Cliopatria's: the pages give 'In the early 19th century, the territory of Kyrgyzstan came under the control of the Khanate of Kokand' and 'In the 1830s, the Khanate of Kokand began to expand northward', and Kokand fortresses at Issyk-Kul, Naryn, Bishkek and Balykchy attacked by Ormon in 1842-1844. The north was held by forts and zakat on herds, so its edge is soft.

correction.text: unchanged shape, years 1848-1852 only; from 1853 the 1856 outline without Ak-Mechet (khanate-of-kokand_1853)

keyframe_review.note: 475,604 km2 for 1848-1855, the same outline. Right to 1852; the Russian conquest page has Ak-Mechet, 'the Kokand Khanate's most influential and critical northern stronghold', captured in 1853 (the plan of January 1853, the departure in June), which takes the lower Syr Darya out of the shape; Cliopatria shows the loss three years late (the 1856 shape begins at 66.3 E).

correction.text: the Kokand lands without Ak-Mechet (Fort Perovsky) on the lower Syr Darya, 411,782 km2

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe 1853-1861: Cliopatria's 1856 outline (411,782 km2, 66.3-80.2 E) applied from the capture of Ak-Mechet in 1853. Dzhulek (1859) and Yany-Kurgan (September 1861) fall on the Syr Darya in these years but are small and are in the ledger only.

411,782 km2 for 1856-1863. Right from 1853 to 1861 (see khanate-of-kokand_1853), but Pishpek and Tokmak are taken in 1862 ('Tokmak and Pishpek were taken in this period') and the Syr Darya towns in 1864, which Cliopatria keeps to 1863.

minus.text: Pishpek and Tokmak, taken by Russia in 1862

correction.text: the 1856 outline without Pishpek and Tokmak

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe 1862-1863: the 1856 outline without the Pishpek-Tokmak country of the Chu valley, taken by Kolpakovsky's force in 1862 ('Russia placed a force at the Kastek pass to block a counterattack from Kokand').

71,142 km2 for 1864-1867 (69.9-74.9 E, 39.4-42.2 N): the Fergana Valley without Khujand, Tashkent and the north. Right from 1866 (Khujand) or 1867 (Kokand page: 'the loss of Khujand followed in 1867'); 1864-1865 are covered by the new keyframes. The Russian conquest page: 'Russia confined the Khanate of Kokand to the Ferghana valley' in 1864-1868. The Kyrgyz highlands round Naryn and At-Bashy (outside the shape) were fought for by Umotaaly 'alongside Kokand allies' until 1867 and are 'formally annexed by the Russian Empire in 1876' (History of Kyrgyzstan): left out as Cliopatria has them; flagged in notes.

correction.text: the Fergana Valley outline of 1864 with Tashkent and Khujand, still Kokandi in 1864

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe for 1864: Turkestan (June 1864) and Aulie-Ata (1864) are gone, but Tashkent (June 1865) and Khujand (1866 on the Russian conquest page, 1867 on the Kokand page) are still Kokand's; Cliopatria's 71,142 km2 shape for 1864 has already lost both. Shymkent changes hands in 1864 on a muddled passage of the page and is left out.

correction.text: the Fergana Valley outline with Khujand, the last Syr Darya town of the khanate before 1866

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe for 1865: Tashkent is taken on 27-29 June 1865 ('on 29 June 1865 Tashkent was taken by the Russian troops of General Chernyayev'); Khujand falls in 1866 (1867 on the Kokand page).

71,252 km2 for 1868-1872, the Fergana Valley: 'The Khanate of Kokand had lost its western territory' and 'remained independent until 1876'. The page does not describe a Russian protectorate; the Kokand page has Khudayar Khan in power until 1875.
71,252 km2 for 1873-1876, the same outline to the Russian annexation: Kaufmann entered the capital on 10 September 1875, the khanate was abolished in 1876 and became the Fergana Oblast.

region.text: the Fergana Valley round the Koktonliq Ata fortress near Kokand

ledger.note: 1709: Shahrukh Biy founds the Khanate of Kokand in the Fergana Valley. 'In 1709, the leader of the Ming tribe, Shahrukh Biy (r. 1709-1722), established the Koktonliq Ata fortress near Kokand'; infobox 'Established: 1709', 'Preceded by: Khanate of Bukhara'. The khanate-of-bukhara dossier has the matching loss.

1734: Urateppe becomes the front with Bukhara. Abd al-Rahim Biy 'briefly seized Khujand, Urateppe, and the remains of Samarkand' and was murdered in Khojand in 1734; 'For 140 years afterward, fighting over Urateppe between Kokand and the Emirate of Bukhara was nearly constant.' The khanate-of-bukhara dossier opens the same contest in 1734.

1740: the capital moves to Kokand. Infobox 'Kokand (1740-1876)'; 'In 1740, Abd al-Karim Biy had the Kokand fortress constructed at the ruins of the old fortress Eski Orda.' (From Koktonliq Ata, 1709-1740.)
1765: Irdana Biy takes Tashkent for a time. Irdana Biy 'temporarily took control of Tashkent in 1765 before Ablay Khan retook it'. The kazakh-khanate dossier has the same two events in 1765.
1765: Ablai Khan retakes Tashkent (same sentence, no month).

1785: the fighting over Urateppe with the Khanate of Bukhara is closed for the dossier chain. The Kokand page has no 1785; the khanate-of-bukhara dossier ends the khanate and this contest in 1785, and the fighting goes on with the Emirate from 1788 (next event).

1788: the Urateppe contest passes to the Emirate of Bukhara. 'For 140 years afterward, fighting over Urateppe between Kokand and the Emirate of Bukhara was nearly constant' (the page names the Emirate; the year is Cliopatria's start of the Emirate row).

1809: Kokand annexes Tashkent. 'In 1809, Tashkent was annexed to the Khanate of Kokand.' The city had been an independent state under Yunus Khoja (1784-1807). Kokand page: Alim 'conquered the western half of the Fergana Valley, taking in Khujand and Tashkent'.

region.text: the Tashkent oasis and the Syr Darya country to Turkestan added by Cliopatria's 1809 shape

ledger.note: 1809: the Syr Darya lands to Turkestan join the Kokand shape. A bridging event: Cliopatria's 1809 shape is 89,000 km2 larger than the Fergana outline, but the Tashkent page dates only Tashkent; the kazakh-khanate dossier has the matching loss for Sayram and Turkestan in 1809.

region.text: the 301,000 km2 added by Cliopatria's 1822 shape: Talas, Chu and Issyk-Kul country and the south-eastern Kazakh steppe

ledger.note: 1822: the Kyrgyz highlands, Talas and the Senior Zhuz steppe join the Kokand shape. A bridging event: the date is Cliopatria's. The pages give only 'In the early 19th century, the territory of Kyrgyzstan came under the control of the Khanate of Kokand' and 'In the 1830s, the Khanate of Kokand began to expand northward'. Part of the land is Kyrgyz tribal country (stateless); the kazakh-khanate dossier has the matching loss for the Kazakh part.

region.text: the Kokand fortresses at Issyk-Kul, Naryn, Bishkek and Balykchy

ledger.note: 1842: the Kyrgyz rise against Kokand's fortresses. 'Rejecting Kokand authority and tribute demands, Ormon launched campaigns against Kokand fortresses in Issyk-Kul, Naryn, Bishkek, and Balykchy between 1842 and 1844'; the Kokand page: the Kyrgyz tribes 'broke away, forming the Kara-Kyrgyz Khanate under the leadership of Ormon Khan'.

region.text: the Fergana Valley round Kokand and Margilan

ledger.note: June 1842: Bukhara occupies Kokand. 'The Emir ... invaded the Khanate in 1842' and Madali Khan was executed on 24 June 1842 by the order of Emir Nasrullah; Shir Ali was installed as khan in June 1842. Earlier: from 1839 the 'Bukhara-Kokand Wars' (Madali page) in which Nasrullah took Istaravshan and Khojend and forced Kokand to pay tribute.

region.text: the Fergana Valley round Kokand and Margilan

ledger.note: August 1842: the Bukharans are driven out. 'The occupation did not last long, and Bukharan forces were exiled two months after the Margilan massacre.' The page gives no month; August is two months after the executions of 24 June 1842 (Kokand page).

region.text: the Kokand fortresses at Issyk-Kul, Naryn, Bishkek and Balykchy

ledger.note: 1844: the last of Ormon's campaigns against the Kokand fortresses ('between 1842 and 1844'); the pages do not say who held Issyk-Kul and Naryn afterwards, and the Russians take Pishpek and Tokmak from Kokand in 1862.

region.text: Ak-Mechet (Fort Perovsky) on the lower Syr Darya

ledger.note: 1853: Russia takes Ak-Mechet. 'In January 1853, the Tsar accepted a plan by Perovsky wherein four forts would be built on the Syr Darya river'; the force left in June; 'The mines were sprung on the 28th, and after a short Russian assault the fort was captured' (Ak-Mechet, 'the Kokand Khanate's most influential and critical northern stronghold'); Khudayar Khan's two attempts to retake it were repulsed.
1859: Dzhulek is taken. 'Dzhulek was taken from Kokand'; the page gives no month.
September 1861: Yany-Kurgan is destroyed. 'Alexander Debu's army took Yany-Kurgan'; the destruction 'deprived the Kokand of a strategic lodgement in the region'.

region.text: Pishpek and Tokmak in the Chu valley

ledger.note: 1862: Pishpek and Tokmak fall. Russia 'placed a force at the Kastek pass to block a counterattack from Kokand. Kolpakovsky then defeated a larger army. Tokmak and Pishpek were taken in this period.' (the year is that of the passage; no month).
1864: Aulie-Ata falls. Chernayev 'led 2500 men from Siberia, and captured Aulie-Ata'. Cliopatria's 1864 shape drops the whole north in this year.
June 1864: Turkestan is lost. 'In June 1864 Veryovkin took Hazrat-i-Turkestan from Kokand.'

29 June 1865: Tashkent falls. 'on 29 June 1865 Tashkent was taken by the Russian troops of General Chernyayev' (the Russian conquest page: a gate opened on 27 June and elders offered surrender on the 29th; the Tashkent page dates the attack to May 1865, and the Kokand regent Alimqul was killed). Tashkent becomes the capital of Russian Turkestan (Kaufmann).

1866: Russia takes Ura-Tepe from Bukhara. Romanovsky 'took Ura-Tepe and Jizzakh from Bukhara' (the page assigns these to Bukhara, not Kokand): the contest between Kokand and the Emirate over Urateppe ends with the Russian conquest, as Kokand's own western lands go the same way.

1866: Khujand falls. Romanovsky 'took Khujand, thus closing the mouth of the Fergana Valley'; the Kokand page has 'the loss of Khujand followed in 1867'. In 1864-1868 Russia 'confined the Khanate of Kokand to the Ferghana valley'.

September 1875: Kaufmann invades the khanate. 'In 1875, the Kokand Khanate rebelled against Russian rule'; Khudayar Khan fled to the Russians at Kojent; 'Kaufmann invaded the Khanate on September 1' and 'entered the capital on 10 September 1875'; Skobelev took command in October and the rebels were beaten at Makhram.
1876: the rebels are executed and the khanate is abolished ('the Russians freely entered Kokand, the leaders of the rebels were executed, and the khanate was abolished').
1876: the Fergana Valley passes to Russia. 'The Khanate of Kokand was declared abolished, and incorporated into the Fergana Oblast of Russian Turkestan.'
1876: the Khanate of Kokand ends. Infobox 'Disestablished: 1876'; 'Succeeded by: Fergana Oblast' (the page gives no month); the last khan named is Nasruddin Khan (1876).

wars.name: Russian conquest of the Khanate of Kokand
wars.outcome: Russian victory: Ak-Mechet (1853), Dzhulek (1859), Yany-Kurgan (1861), Pishpek and Tokmak (1862), Turkestan and Aulie-Ata (1864), Tashkent (1865), Khujand (1866); in 1875-76 the khanate is annexed as the Fergana Oblast.
wars.note: Kokand 'continued to launch small attacks and raids well into the 1860s'.

wars.name: Bukhara-Kokand wars
wars.outcome: Near-constant fighting over Urateppe for 'a 140-year' span; in 1839-1842 Emir Nasrullah took Istaravshan and Khojend, made Kokand pay tribute, invaded in 1842 and executed Madali Khan; Russia took Ura-Tepe and Jizzakh from Bukhara in 1866.
wars.note: Madali page: the wars 'initiated in 1839 when Kokand built a fort close to Bukhara'. Frontier changes between 1734 and 1842 are not dated on the pages.

wars.name: Kyrgyz rising under Ormon

zones.text: the Kokand fortresses at Issyk-Kul, Naryn, Bishkek and Balykchy

wars.outcome: Ormon's campaigns against the Kokand fortresses at Issyk-Kul, Naryn, Bishkek and Balykchy; the Kara-Kyrgyz Khanate 'broke away'; the pages do not say who held the fortresses afterwards.

wars.name: Dzungar invasions of Kokand
wars.outcome: 'The Dzungars invaded Kokand in 1742 and 1745 and were repelled'; no frontier moved.

wars.name: Kokand-Kazakh struggle for Tashkent
wars.outcome: Irdana Biy took Tashkent 'temporarily ... in 1765 before Ablay Khan retook it'.

certainty.note: Fergana core by its valley walls; the northern conquests are held by forts and zakat on herds, and the Bukhara frontier at Urateppe and Khujand moves in raids.

The Russian advance is dated by captured forts and towns (Ak-Mechet 1853, Turkestan 1864, Tashkent 1865, Khujand 1866); no page gives a boundary line, not even for the confinement to the Fergana valley of 1864-1868.

notes:
Cliopatria row reviewed: Khanate of Kokand (1709-1876, 11 shapes) plus four new keyframes (1853, 1862, 1864, 1865). Page budget five (Kokand, Russian conquest of Central Asia, Tashkent, Madali Khan, History of Kyrgyzstan), a sixth page (Dzungar Khanate) used for one war only.

Shape-by-shape: the growth to 174,694 km2 (1809) is explained for Tashkent only; the growth to 475,816 km2 (1822) and the Syr Darya and Kazakh-steppe part of 1809 are on no page opened and are recorded as confidence-1 bridging gains with the kazakh-khanate dossier's matching losses as counterpart (its losses of 1809 and 1822 are Cliopatria's too). The shrink of 1856 is the loss of Ak-Mechet in 1853, three years earlier (page); the shrink of 1864 puts Tashkent (1865) and Khujand (1866/67) a year or two early (page), so intermediate keyframes were added. Not drawn: Shymkent (muddled passage of the Russian conquest page); the Kyrgyz highlands at Naryn, At-Bashy and Issyk-Kul, which Cliopatria drops in 1864 but which the History of Kyrgyzstan page puts under Kokand until the 'formal annexation' of 1876 (Ormon's Kara-Kyrgyz Khanate had risen against the Kokand fortresses in 1842-1844 and Umotaaly fought to 1867). Kokand's status as a Russian dependent after 1868 is on no page opened (the Russian conquest page does not describe a vassalage), so there is no vassal event; the Qing relation (Irdana Biy's embassy under Qianlong, the 1809 apology and reconciliation, Jahangir Khoja housed at Kokand) moves no frontier on the Kokand page.

Dates in conflict: Tashkent's fall (attack May 1865 on the Tashkent page, 27/29 June on the Russian conquest page, 29 June on the Kokand page); Khujand (1866, Russian conquest page; 1867, Kokand page); infobox rulers (Abd al-Rahim 1723-1733, Shir Ali 1842-1845, Khudayar 1845-1875) against the table (1722-1734, 1842-1844, 1844-1858/1862-63/1865-75). Reigns 1858-1862 and 1863-1865 were not read.

Counterparts without dossiers: tashkent-state (Yunus Khoja's Tashkent, 1784-1807; ia-03-x); kara-kyrgyz-khanate (Ormon, from 1842; ia-03-x or the Central Asia additions); emirate-of-bukhara and khanate-of-bukhara have dossiers (other parts of ia-03). Gazetteer: all names resolve; 'Margilan' and 'Dzhulek' are not places (a radius round Qyzylorda is used for the Syr Darya forts).

Area check: infobox '647,497 km2' for the late 1830s against 475,816 km2: ratio 0.73, kept.
